---
title: "Follow-up forms are reports, not events"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = FALSE
)
```

SRTR follow-up files (`TXF_KI`, `TXF_LI`, and so on) hold one row per
follow-up form. It is tempting to read them as a clinical record: find the
first form that says "yes", take its date, and call that the event. That
reading is wrong in several ways, and each one quietly changes an
analysis. This article walks through them with code you can run on your own
standard analysis files (SAFs). The companion article,
[Follow-up windows and death](follow-up-windows.html), covers what happens
around the end of follow-up and death.

# Which section answers your question

Each outcome is spread across both articles. This table points to the
sections that matter for each one.

| Outcome | Sections |
|---|---|
| Rejection, treated or untreated | ["Rejection" has more than one meaning](#rejection-has-more-than-one-meaning); [Rejection during the transplant admission](#rejection-during-the-transplant-admission-is-not-on-the-follow-up-forms); [Rejection after the graft has failed](follow-up-windows.html#rejection-after-the-graft-has-failed) |
| Malignancy | [A form date is not an onset date](#a-form-date-is-not-an-onset-date); [A missing date does not mean "no event"](#a-missing-date-does-not-mean-no-event); [Reports dated on the day of death](follow-up-windows.html#reports-dated-on-the-day-of-death) |
| Graft failure | [Graft failure and death on the same day](follow-up-windows.html#graft-failure-and-death-on-the-same-day); [Whose follow-up?](follow-up-windows.html#whose-follow-up) |
| Death | [Which death date?](follow-up-windows.html#which-death-date); [Deaths found after follow-up ends](follow-up-windows.html#deaths-found-after-follow-up-ends) |
| When follow-up ends | [Events count only while someone is watching](follow-up-windows.html#events-count-only-while-someone-is-watching); [Whose follow-up?](follow-up-windows.html#whose-follow-up) |
| People or transplants | [Count registrations, and say so](#count-registrations-and-say-so); [Transplants are not people](files-and-keys.html#transplants-are-not-people) |

The code here is not run on this website, because it needs real SAFs. You
can run it yourself: each section shows a naive version first, then the
sRtr function that handles the problem. Every chunk prints counts, never
rows, and masks any count from 1 to 10 with the `mask()` and `mask_n()`
helpers below. Masking each number is not enough on its own: a total shared
beside masked parts, or two counts that differ by a little, gives a small
count away. [Share counts only](checking-your-safs.html#share-counts-only)
explains the rules; follow them when you adapt the code.

```{r setup}
library(sRtr)
library(dplyr)

set_srtr_wd("path/to/your/SAFs")

tx <- load_srtr_file("TX_LI")
txf <- load_srtr_file(
  "TXF_LI",
  col_select = c(
    "TRR_ID", "ORG_TY", "TFL_PX_STAT_DT", "TFL_FOL_CD",
    "TFL_MALIG", "TFL_ACUTE_REJ_EPISODE"
  )
)

# Counts safe to share: any count from 1 to 10 shows as "<11".
mask_n <- function(n) {
  noquote(ifelse(n > 0 & n < 11, "<11", format(n, big.mark = ",")))
}
# The same for a column of categories; never identifiers or dates.
mask <- function(x) mask_n(table(x, useNA = "ifany"))
```

The examples use liver files and malignancy and acute rejection, the two
outcomes `add_txf_outcomes()` derives. The same issues apply to the other
organs. For background on where SRTR data come from and how they are
collected, see [Leppke et al. 2013](#ref-leppke) and
[Massie et al. 2014](#ref-massie).

# A form date is not an onset date

Each follow-up form covers a period, often a year, and its date
(`TFL_PX_STAT_DT`, the patient status date) is when the status was
recorded. A form that first says "yes, malignancy" after one that said
"no" tells you the *recorded* status changed between those two dates.
Transplant programs file these forms at 6 months and then every year after
transplant, until the recipient dies or the graft fails
([OPTN 2021](#ref-optn2021)). The forms do not ask when a rejection
happened, so SRTR staff describe the incidence of rejection as a "step"
function ([Kim and Snyder 2012](#ref-kim2012), slide 33).

That interval bounds when the malignancy began only if the forms are
complete and timely: if each form records what was known at the time, and
a malignancy is recorded on the first form after it is found. A
malignancy recognized late, or present but not recorded on an earlier
form, can have begun before the interval. Read the interval as bounding
the change in recorded status, and treat it as bounding onset only as an
assumption you state. The figure below shows three made-up recipients.

```{r timeline, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Timeline of follow-up forms for three made-up recipients, in years since transplant. Recipient A has forms saying no at years 1 and 2 and yes at year 3; the recorded status changed somewhere in the shaded interval between years 2 and 3. Recipient B has a form saying no at year 1, an unknown answer at year 2 and yes at year 3; the recorded status changed somewhere between years 1 and 3. Recipient C has forms saying unknown at years 1 and 2, so nothing is known about malignancy. The interval bounds onset only if the forms are complete and timely."}
forms <- data.frame(
  who = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), c(3, 3, 2)),
  year = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2),
  answer = c("No", "No", "Yes", "No", "Unknown", "Yes", "Unknown", "Unknown")
)
forms$answer <- factor(forms$answer, c("No", "Yes", "Unknown"))
intervals <- data.frame(who = c("A", "B"), from = c(2, 1), to = c(3, 3))
ink <- "#52514e"

ggplot2::ggplot(forms, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = who)) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    data = intervals,
    ggplot2::aes(x = from, xend = to, y = who, yend = who),
    linewidth = 6, colour = "#cde2fb", lineend = "round"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    ggplot2::aes(colour = answer, shape = answer),
    size = 3.5, stroke = 1.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text", x = 0.05, y = 3.45, label = "Transplant",
    hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink
  ) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text", x = 2.5, y = 3.32, label = "Recorded status changed in here",
    size = 3.2, colour = ink
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(No = "#2a78d6", Yes = "#eb6834", Unknown = "#8a8984"),
    name = "Form says"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(No = 16, Yes = 17, Unknown = 1),
    name = "Form says"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(limits = c("C", "B", "A")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    "Years since transplant", breaks = 0:3, limits = c(0, 3.2)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "Recipient") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )
```

**The naive approach** takes the first "yes":

```{r}
naive <- txf |>
  filter(TFL_MALIG == "Y") |>
  summarise(malig_date = min(TFL_PX_STAT_DT), .by = TRR_ID)
```

This gives the date of the first *report*, which comes after the change
in status, by up to the gap between forms. It also has a technical trap: `min()` returns `NA` for a
recipient whose positive forms include an undated one, and with
`na.rm = TRUE` it returns `Inf`, with a warning, when all of them are
undated.

**With sRtr**, `add_txf_outcomes()` gives the first report date and the
other end of the interval: the last form that explicitly said "no" before
it.

```{r}
tx <- add_txf_outcomes(tx)

gap <- as.numeric(tx$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE - tx$FIRST_FU_MALIG_LAST_NEG_DATE)
mask_n(sum(!is.na(gap)))

# For your own inspection; share only if the count above is large.
gap_quartiles <- quantile(gap, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
```

On real files the median gap is close to a year, because forms are mostly
annual. An analysis that treats the report date as the event date is
right-censored data with a built-in delay; the two dates together support
interval-censored or discrete-time models instead, under the assumption
above. Assigning each event to the end (or start, or middle) of its
interval and then using standard survival methods "can lead to invalid
inferences" and tends to understate standard errors
([Lindsey and Ryan 1998](#ref-lindsey)). An SRTR example is
[Levitsky et al. 2017](#ref-levitsky). Their SRTR data recorded only
whether biopsy-proven rejection had occurred since the last assessment.
They therefore modeled time to first rejection with discrete-time survival
analysis. When rejection was a time-dependent covariate, they imputed its
date from a uniform distribution within the reporting interval, using five
imputations.

# A missing date does not mean "no event"

**The naive approach** joins the first dates back to the cohort and calls
everyone without one event-free:

```{r}
naive_cohort <- tx |>
  left_join(naive, by = "TRR_ID") |>
  mutate(malignancy = !is.na(malig_date))
```

That merges four quite different groups into "no malignancy":

- recipients whose forms said "no";
- recipients whose forms said only "unknown" or were left blank;
- recipients with no follow-up form at all;
- recipients with a "yes" form that has no date.

**With sRtr**, the status column keeps them apart:

```{r}
mask(tx$FIRST_FU_MALIG_STATUS)
```

`"event"` means at least one form reports a malignancy, dated or not;
`"no event"` means none does and at least one says "no"; `"unknown"` means
there are forms but none says "yes" or "no"; `"no follow-up"` means there is
no form. On real liver files, "unknown" and "no follow-up" are each large
groups, not rounding errors. Whether to exclude them, treat them as
censored at transplant, or model them is an analysis decision, and it
should be made on purpose. Loss to follow-up is common in the long term:
in a study of children who received a liver transplant, 1 in 6 of those
who had not died or been retransplanted were reported as lost to follow-up
([Cheng et al. 2022](#ref-cheng)).

The forms also miss events, so "no event" means "none reported". Compared
with linked cancer registries, SRTR identified about half of the cancers
studied ([Yanik et al. 2016](#ref-yanik)); studies of cancer after
transplant often link SRTR to cancer registries instead
([Engels et al. 2011](#ref-engels)). For
liver rejection, [Levitsky et al. 2017](#ref-levitsky) found more rejections
missing from SRTR than missing from their research cohort. Forms due during
the COVID-19 emergency are another gap. For forms due from 13 March 2020 to
31 March 2021, OPTN accepted non-submission of the full follow-up form, but
still required notice of death or graft failure. The notice ending this
relaxation required forms left unsubmitted to be completed by 1 July 2021
([OPTN 2021](#ref-optn2021)). So a form from that period may have been
filed late, or not at all. Check how complete those forms are in your
release.

# "Rejection" has more than one meaning

The rejection question (`TFL_ACUTE_REJ_EPISODE`, format `ACREJEPF`) has
four answers: 1, at least one episode treated with an anti-rejection
agent; 2, rejection, none treated; 3, no; 998, unknown.

**The naive approach** matches the label text:

```{r}
naive_rej <- txf |>
  filter(
    TFL_ACUTE_REJ_EPISODE ==
      "1: Yes, at least one episode treated with anti-rejection agent"
  )
mask_n(nrow(naive_rej))
```

This finds nothing if the file was loaded with raw codes
(`factor_labels = FALSE`), and nothing if SRTR rewords the label in a later
release. And it treats an untreated rejection (code 2) the same as "no".

**With sRtr**, rejection is matched by code, so raw and labelled files give
the same answer, and an untreated rejection gets its own status:

```{r}
mask(tx$FIRST_FU_REJ_STATUS)
```

The derived endpoint is *treated* acute rejection. An untreated rejection
is evidence that rejection happened, so it is never used as a negative form
when bounding the interval in `FIRST_FU_REJ_LAST_NEG_DATE`.

# Rejection during the transplant admission is not on the follow-up forms

Rejection before discharge is recorded on the transplant record
(`REC_ACUTE_REJ_EPISODE` in `TX_LI`), not on a follow-up form, and it has
no date of its own.

**The naive approach** uses only the follow-up file, and so misses early
rejection, or counts it late, at the first follow-up form.

**With sRtr**, `add_time_to_event_outcomes()` (see the note in
[Follow-up windows and death](follow-up-windows.html)) uses the admission
rejection first. It
dates it at discharge, a proxy: the transplant date plus the length of stay
(`REC_POSTX_LOS`), else the discharge date (`REC_DISCHRG_DT`).
`FIRST_REJ_DATE_SOURCE` records which rule applied:

```{r}
out <- add_time_to_event_outcomes(tx)
mask(out$FIRST_REJ_DATE_SOURCE)
```

When neither date is usable, the rejection still counts: its status is 1
and its time is missing, so it drops out of a survival model rather than
adding rejection-free time. The same rule covers a rejection or malignancy
reported only on undated follow-up forms. Each case gives a warning with
the count.

# Forms can be dated before the transplant

A follow-up form describes the period after transplant, so a form dated
before it is a data error. Check how many you have:

```{r}
tx_date <- tx$REC_TX_DT[match(txf$TRR_ID, tx$TRR_ID)]
mask_n(sum(txf$TFL_PX_STAT_DT < tx_date, na.rm = TRUE))
```

In liver files they are rare, but a single one can matter: with the naive
approach, a pre-transplant "yes" becomes an event at time zero, or a
negative time. sRtr times events from the first report on or after the
transplant date; the date columns from `add_txf_outcomes()` keep the first
report of all, so you can find these cases.

# Count registrations, and say so

Each row of a transplant file is a transplant registration (`TRR_ID`), not
a person. A person transplanted twice has two rows, and two sets of
follow-up forms.

```{r}
# Complete, distinct pairs of registration and person.
ids <- tx |>
  filter(!is.na(TRR_ID), !is.na(PERS_ID)) |>
  distinct(TRR_ID, PERS_ID)
one_person_per_registration <- !anyDuplicated(ids$TRR_ID)
one_person_per_registration
# Print only the masked repeat count, and only if the check passes.
if (one_person_per_registration) {
  mask_n(c(repeat_registrations = nrow(ids) - n_distinct(ids$PERS_ID)))
}
```

`repeat_registrations` counts registrations after a person's first one.
Keep the registration total for yourself: shared beside it, the repeat
count gives away the number of people. This is the same check as in
[Check the keys](checking-your-safs.html#check-the-keys).

`add_txf_outcomes()` attaches a report of the merge, in registrations: how
many registrations have any follow-up form, how many forms were read and
how many were undated, and for each outcome the positive forms, the
registrations with a report, and the registrations whose report is dated.
These counts are nested, so the difference between two of them can be a
small count. Look at the report yourself, and before you put any of it in
a methods section, check that no such difference is under 11.

```{r}
# For your own inspection.
report <- attr(tx, "txf_report")
mask_n(unlist(report[setdiff(names(report), c("follow_up_file", "outcomes"))]))
report$outcomes |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), mask_n))
```

The report describes the cohort at the time of the merge; filter first,
then call `add_txf_outcomes()`, if you want it to describe your analysis
cohort.

# Checklist

- Treat follow-up dates as report dates. The last negative form and the
  first report bound a change in recorded status; say so if you treat them
  as bounding onset.
- Read the status column before treating a missing date as no event.
- Decide what "unknown" and "no follow-up" mean for your question.
- Match codes, not label text, and decide whether untreated rejection
  counts.
- Include rejection during the transplant admission.
- Look for forms dated before the transplant.
- Report counts in registrations, and mask counts under 11 when you share
  them.
